detailed_html:
NCERT CLASS 12 • TOPIC 12 OF 13

12. Ecosystem

01 1. Ecosystem Architecture & Stratification Principles

ECOSYSTEM STRUCTURE & PRIMARY PRODUCTIVITY
DECOMPOSITION DYNAMICS (5 STEPS)
NEET High-Yield Focus Point

Productivity Equation: $NPP = GPP - R$. Whole biosphere annual Net Primary Productivity = ~170 billion tons (dry organic weight). Oceans cover ~70% of Earth surface, yet contribute ONLY 55 billion tons (~32%) due to light attenuation and nitrogen/iron limitations.

Clinical & Biological Application

Robert Costanza Ecological Pricing (1997): Put an average price tag of US $33 trillion per year on fundamental ecosystem services (nearly double global GNP of $18 trillion). Soil formation accounts for ~50%, recreation ~10%, climate regulation ~6%.

Memory Mnemonic

5 Steps of Decomposition: F-L-C-H-M → Fragmentation (Earthworms) → Leaching (Water-soluble minerals) → Catabolism (Enzymes) → Humification (Dark humus) → Mineralization (Inorganic release).

NCERT Diagram Breakdown
NCERT Fig 12.4 Ecological Pyramids: Pyramid of numbers in grassland (upright: millions of grasses → thousands of insects → few hawks); Pyramid of biomass in ocean (inverted: 4 g/m² phytoplankton → 21 g/m² fishes).

02 2. Primary Productivity (GPP vs NPP) & Biomass Yields

Decomposition Kinetics: Slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin; faster if rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars. Warm, moist environments dramatically accelerate decomposition; low temperatures and anaerobiosis inhibit it.
ENERGY FLOW & FOOD CHAINS
NEET High-Yield Focus Point

Decomposition Rate Regulators: Warm and moist environment dramatically accelerates decomposition. Lignin and chitin rich detritus decomposes very slowly; nitrogen and water-soluble sugars rich detritus decomposes extremely rapidly.

Clinical & Biological Application

Eutrophication & Algal Blooms: Runoff rich in nitrogen and phosphorus leads to accelerated aging of lakes (cultural eutrophication); massive cyanobacterial blooms deplete dissolved oxygen, choking aquatic life.

Memory Mnemonic

Hydrarch Succession Stages: Please Save Free Rivers, Marsh Seems Fantastic → Phytoplankton → Submerged → Floating → Reed swamp → Marsh meadow → Scrub → Forest.

03 3. Decomposition Cascade: 5 Sequential Steps

NCERT Comparison: Ecological Pyramids
ECOLOGICAL SUCCESSION: HYDRARCH & XERARCH
NEET High-Yield Focus Point

Pyramid of Energy Universal Law: The Pyramid of Energy is ALWAYS upright and can NEVER be inverted, because energy is inevitably dissipated as metabolic heat at every successive trophic step under the Second Law of Thermodynamics.

04 4. Trophic Energy Dynamics & Ecological Pyramids

Refer to detailed study notes and high-yield callouts below.

NEET High-Yield Focus Point

Inverted Biomass Pyramid in Oceans: The pyramid of biomass in sea is typically inverted because the standing crop biomass of short-lived microscopic phytoplankton is far smaller than that of long-lived herbivorous and carnivorous fishes.

05 5. Ecological Succession: Hydrarch & Xerarch Sequences

Refer to detailed study notes and high-yield callouts below.

NEET High-Yield Focus Point

Succession Convergence to Mesic: Both Hydrarch succession (originating in deep water) and Xerarch succession (originating on bare rock) progressively evolve towards the identical medium water condition: a stable Mesic climax forest community!
revision_html:
High-Yield Revision — Ecosystem

  • Productivity: $NPP = GPP - R$. Biosphere annual NPP = 170 billion tons (oceans contribute only 55 billion tons despite 70% area).
  • Decomposition Steps: Fragmentation (earthworm) $\to$ Leaching $\to$ Catabolism (enzymes) $\to$ Humification (humus) $\to$ Mineralization.
  • Energy Flow: PAR < 50% solar radiation; plants capture 2-10% PAR. Lindeman's 10% law.
  • Aquatic vs Terrestrial Conduit: Aquatic = GFC major conduit; Terrestrial = DFC major conduit.
  • Pyramids: Energy is ALWAYS upright. Biomass is INVERTED in sea/ocean (phytoplankton < zooplankton/fish). Numbers inverted on single tree.
  • Succession: Both Hydrarch (wet) and Xerarch (dry) converge to stable Mesic Forest climax. Pioneer on rock = Lichens; Pioneer in water = Phytoplankton.

flashcards.q: Why is the annual net primary productivity of oceans only 55 billion tons despite covering 70% of Earth?
flashcards.a: Due to limited light penetration in deep waters and severe scarcity of essential mineral nutrients (like nitrogen and iron) across vast open pelagic zones.

flashcards.q: What are the 5 sequential steps of the decomposition process?
flashcards.a: 1. Fragmentation (detritivores), 2. Leaching (water-soluble salts wash down), 3. Catabolism (microbial enzymes), 4. Humification (dark amorphous humus formation), and 5. Mineralization (inorganic nutrient release).

flashcards.q: Why is the Pyramid of Energy always strictly upright without any exceptions?
flashcards.a: According to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, energy is irreversibly dissipated as respiratory metabolic heat at each trophic transfer; thus, higher trophic levels invariably receive less energy.

flashcards.q: Under what condition is the Pyramid of Biomass inverted?
flashcards.a: In aquatic/marine ecosystems, where the standing crop biomass of phytoplankton producers is smaller than that of zooplanktons and fishes due to the phytoplanktons' microscopic size, rapid life cycle, and high turnover rate.

flashcards.q: What are the pioneer species in Xerarch succession versus Hydrarch succession?
flashcards.a: In Xerarch succession on bare rock, pioneer species are lichens (secreting weathering acids). In Hydrarch succession in water, pioneer species are microscopic phytoplanktons.

flashcards.q: What is the ultimate climatic endpoint of both Hydrarch and Xerarch succession?
flashcards.a: Both successional pathways converge on a medium moisture (Mesic) climax community, typically a stable mature forest.

detailed_html:
NCERT CLASS 12 • TOPIC 13 OF 13

13. Biodiversity and Conservation

01 1. Biodiversity Hierarchies & Global Distribution Patterns

BIODIVERSITY LEVELS & GLOBAL ESTIMATES
NEET High-Yield Focus Point

Levels of Biodiversity:
• Genetic Diversity: Rauwolfia vomitoria in Himalayas shows variation in active chemical Reserpine; India has >50,000 distinct strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.
• Species Diversity: Western Ghats harbor greater amphibian species richness than Eastern Ghats.
• Ecological Diversity: India has higher ecosystem diversity (deserts, rainforests, mangroves, coral reefs) than Scandinavian countries like Norway.

Clinical & Biological Application

Paul Ehrlich Rivet Popper Hypothesis: Ecosystem is an airplane; thousands of species are rivets holding parts together. Removing a rivet (species extinction) might not cause crash immediately, but popping rivets from wings (keystone species, e.g. primary pollinators) causes catastrophic flight failure and ecosystem collapse.

Memory Mnemonic

The Evil Quartet Drivers: H-O-A-C → Habitat loss & fragmentation, Over-exploitation, Alien species invasion, Co-extinction.

NCERT Diagram Breakdown
NCERT Fig 13.1 Global Biodiversity Invertebrates/Vertebrates/Plants: Invertebrates: Insects occupy more than half of the pie chart followed by other animal groups, molluscs, and crustaceans; Plants: Fungi and Angiosperms represent largest segments.

02 2. Latitudinal Gradients & Humboldt's Species-Area Power Law

PATTERNS OF BIODIVERSITY & SPECIES-AREA RELATIONSHIP
NEET High-Yield Focus Point

Robert May Global Estimate: Mathematically sound global species estimate is ~7 million species. Only 1.5 million currently cataloged. Animals constitute >70% of all recorded species, while plants make up ~22%. Insects make up >70% of all animals (7 out of 10 animals are insects!). Species of fungi exceed the combined total of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals!

Clinical & Biological Application

International Environmental Treaties: Earth Summit (Rio de Janeiro, 1992 → Convention on Biological Diversity); World Summit on Sustainable Development (Johannesburg, 2002 → 190 countries committed to significant reduction in biodiversity loss rate).

Memory Mnemonic

Extinct Species NCERT List: D-Q-T-S-P → Dodo (Mauritius), Quagga (Africa), Thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia), Passenger pigeon.

03 3. Ecological Stability Experiments & Rivet Popper Hypothesis

LOSS OF BIODIVERSITY: THE "EVIL QUARTET"
NEET High-Yield Focus Point

Species-Area Relationship (Alexander von Humboldt): On logarithmic scale, $\log S = \log C + Z \log A$. Slope $Z$ is 0.1 to 0.2 regardless of taxonomic group in small regions; for entire continents, $Z$ is much steeper: 0.6 to 1.2 (e.g. frugivorous birds in tropical forests $Z = 1.15$).

04 4. Biodiversity Loss: The Evil Quartet

BIODIVERSITY CONSERVATION STRATEGIES:
  • Why Conserve?
    • Narrowly Utilitarian: Direct economic benefits: food (cereals, pulses), firewood, fiber, construction, industrial tannins/dyes, $>25\%$ of prescription drugs derived from plants (Bioprospecting).
    • Broadly Utilitarian: Ecosystem services: Amazon produces $20\%$ of Earth's $O_2$; pollination by bees; flood/erosion control; aesthetic joy.
    • Ethical: Moral responsibility to preserve all living species for future generations.
  • In-Situ (On-Site) Conservation: Protecting endangered species in their natural habitat:
    • Biodiversity Hotspots: Regions with exceptionally high species richness and high degree of endemism (species confined to that region and found nowhere else). 34 hotspots worldwide covering $<2\%$ of Earth's land, but strict protection reduces extinction by $30\%$. 3 Hotspots cover India: 1. Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, 2. Indo-Burma, 3. Himalaya.
    • Protected Areas in India: 14 Biosphere Reserves, 90 National Parks, 448 Wildlife Sanctuaries.
    • Sacred Groves: Undisturbed forest patches protected by tribal religious traditions: Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya (last refuges for rare plants), Aravalli Hills in Rajasthan, Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, Sarguja, Chanda, Bastar in MP.
  • Ex-Situ (Off-Site) Conservation: Threatened animals and plants taken out of natural habitat and placed in special care settings:
    • Zoological Parks, Botanical Gardens, Wildlife Safari Parks.
    • Advanced biotechnological methods: Cryopreservation of gametes in liquid nitrogen at $-196^\circ\text{C}$ in viable form; In vitro fertilization; Tissue culture propagation; Seed Banks.
  • International Conventions:
    • The Earth Summit (Rio de Janeiro, 1992): Convention on Biological Diversity calling all nations to conserve biodiversity.
    • World Summit on Sustainable Development (Johannesburg, South Africa, 2002): 190 countries pledged commitment to significantly reduce biodiversity loss rate.
NEET High-Yield Focus Point

The Evil Quartet (Drivers of Extinction):
1. Habitat Loss & Fragmentation: Most critical cause (Amazon rainforest cut for soybeans and cattle ranching).
2. Over-exploitation: Steller’s sea cow, passenger pigeon driven extinct by human greed.
3. Alien Species Invasions: Nile perch in Lake Victoria killed >200 cichlid fish; Eichhornia (water hyacinth), Parthenium (carrot grass), Lantana; African catfish Clarias gariepinus.
4. Co-extinctions: Obligate mutualisms (e.g. co-evolved plant-pollinator mutualism).

05 5. Conservation Strategies: In-Situ vs Ex-Situ Conservation

Refer to detailed study notes and high-yield callouts below.

NEET High-Yield Focus Point

In-situ vs Ex-situ Conservation:
• In-situ (On-site): 34 Biodiversity Hotspots covering <2% of Earth's land, reducing mass extinction by ~30% (India has 3: Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya); 14 Biosphere reserves, 90 National parks, 448 Wildlife sanctuaries, Sacred groves (Khasi & Jaintia hills).
• Ex-situ (Off-site): Botanical gardens, zoological parks, wildlife safari, seed banks, Cryopreservation at −196°C in liquid nitrogen.

flashcards.q: What is the mathematical equation for Alexander von Humboldt's Species-Area Relationship?
flashcards.a: log S = log C + Z log A, where S is species richness, A is area, C is the y-intercept, and Z is the regression coefficient (slope of the line).

flashcards.q: What are the four major causes of biodiversity loss collectively known as 'The Evil Quartet'?
flashcards.a: 1. Habitat loss and fragmentation, 2. Over-exploitation, 3. Alien species invasions, and 4. Co-extinctions.

flashcards.q: Name the three biodiversity hotspots that extend into India's geographical territory.
flashcards.a: 1. Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, 2. Indo-Burma, and 3. Himalaya.

flashcards.q: What is an ecological endemic species?
flashcards.a: A species that is confined exclusively to a particular geographic region and is not found anywhere else in the world.

flashcards.q: Give two prominent examples of animal species driven to extinction by over-exploitation.
flashcards.a: Steller's Sea Cow and the Passenger Pigeon.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between In-Situ and Ex-Situ conservation? Give two examples of each.
flashcards.a: In-situ protects species within their natural ecosystem (National Parks, Biosphere Reserves). Ex-situ protects endangered species outside their natural habitat (Cryopreservation, Zoological Parks).

pages.text: Biodiversity levels: Genetic diversity in Rauwolfia vomitoria producing reserpine, species diversity in Western Ghats amphibians, ecological diversity in Indian rainforests and deserts. Robert May estimated 7 million species with animals over 70% and insects making up 70% of animals. India has 8.1% of global biodiversity.

Patterns of biodiversity: Tropics harbor more species than temperate zones with Amazon rainforest highest. Humboldt species-area relationship log S equals log C plus Z log A with Z between 0.1 and 0.2 for regions and 0.6 to 1.2 for continents. Tilman proved diversity increases ecosystem stability.

The Evil Quartet causing biodiversity loss: habitat loss in Amazon forest, over-exploitation causing extinction of Steller's sea cow and passenger pigeon, alien species invasions like Nile perch and water hyacinth, and co-extinctions. Conservation in-situ includes 34 hotspots and sacred groves; ex-situ includes cryopreservation at -196°C and seed banks.
